newsitem.title: UK: British financial advisers urge regulatory revamp.
newsitem.headline: British financial advisers urge regulatory revamp.

text.p: Britain's Independent Financial Advisers Association on Tuesday called for a major overhaul of the regulation of retail financial services in Britain.

The trade association, which represents more than 2,300 firms of independent financial advisers and some 7,000 registered individuals, said financial services regulation is "ill defined, poorly targeted and mis-understood by the public".
"It is absolutely crucial that we have a system of regulation that the public understands and where responsibilities are clearly defined," Garry Heath, the body's chief executive said in a statement.

He said regulators had tried to make the market place safer by putting increasing burden on advisers and salesmen. But in shifting the burden from the buyer to the seller, they had increased the cost of financial products.
This in turn meant that "those on lower incomes are less likely to be able to afford proper advice".

The association, which was set up in 1994, said the only way to gain public confidence was through fundamental changes to the scope of the Financial Services Act and to the system of regulation itself.

It said that unnecessary layers of regulation need to be eliminated and a single-tier statutory regulator, directly accountable to parliament, created to remove the current fragmentation of responsibilities.

Britain's opposition Labour party, which is leading in the polls ahead of the May 1 election, has said it would merge the existing regulatory bodies with top financial watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) if it is elected.
Under the 1986 Financial Services Act, regulation is carried out by three "frontline" regulators.
The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), the Personal Investment Authority (PIA) and the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) are all supervised by the SIB.

Questions about the effectiveness of this system have been raised by Britain's pensions mis-selling scandal and high-profile financial scandals such as the collapse of Barings in February 1995 and subsequent problems at other firms.

On Monday Sir Andrew Large, retiring chairman of the SIB, said it would shortly publish a discussion paper seeking industry views on making senior executives more acccountable as well as lightening the regulatory load for firms acting responsibly.
The association also argued for an open process of consultation "to ensure that the arguments of consumers, the industry and the secretariat are incorporated into policy formation".

It said that disclosure should be widened to include products currently outside the scope of the Financial Services Act. This could include a product specific industry average to alert customers who do not shop around to the costs associated with the product they are purchasing.
Customers should also be encouraged to ask about the changing nature of the products they are about to buy, the association said.

And a profound change away from detailed rules towards regulatory principles supported by detailed guidance was also required, it added. This question is due to be addressed in the SIB's discussion document as part of a reappraisal of the balance between principles and prescription.

The association said that the Audit Commission should be brought in to provide regular external checks on the cost-effectiveness of regulation and effective deterrents to mis-selling and fraud needed to be established.
Failure to meet with minimum standards should be met by penalties for those responsible, including the principals and directors of the firm, it said.
